parts: Look at the window next time you're on an airplane.
Notice something strange?
It isn't square. It has no sharp corners, just a smooth, rounded shape.
Almost every airliner flying today has windows like this.
And that tiny design detail is far more important than you might imagine.
A window is usually a rectangle. Four straight sides. Four neat corners. It's the easiest shape to cut, to fit, and to frame.
So why would airplane designers choose something harder?
Because an airplane isn't a house. At cruising altitude the air outside is far too thin to breathe, so the cabin is pressurized.
On every flight, the fuselage is pushed outward from the inside, a little like a balloon. On every landing, it relaxes again.
Thousands of flights. Thousands of tiny stretches. Each one harmless on its own.
In the early 1950s, Britain built something the world had never seen: the de Havilland Comet, one of the world's first jet airliners.
It was fast. It was smooth. It flew above the weather. Passengers had never travelled like this.
Its windows were large and nearly square, with only slightly rounded corners.
At the time, nothing about those windows looked like a warning sign.
Then, in 1954, two Comets broke apart in mid-air, within three months of each other.
On the tenth of January, a Comet came apart in flight near the island of Elba. Thirty-five people died.
On the eighth of April, another one broke up near Naples. Twenty-one more lives were lost.
This time, the entire fleet was grounded indefinitely.
These were young aircraft, and the cause was far from obvious. Investigators had to find out what had broken them.
So engineers did something remarkable. They took a real Comet fuselage and sank it into a giant tank of water.
Then they pressurized it, and relaxed it, again and again, repeating the strain of flight over and over.
After thousands of cycles, it failed. And the crack began at the corner of a window.
In the wreckage, the story was similar. The trouble started at the corners of squarish openings in the fuselage, including the windows for a radio antenna on the roof.
The problem wasn't simply the glass. It was what those corners could do to the metal surrounding them.
To understand why, we have to look at something completely invisible: stress.
When a fuselage is pulled outward, the force doesn't sit still. It flows through the metal skin, a little like water flowing down a river.
Where the metal is smooth and unbroken, that flow is calm and evenly spread.
But cut a hole in it, and the flow has to bend around the hole.
At a sharp corner, it can't turn smoothly. The lines of force crowd together and squeeze through a tiny spot, and that spot carries far more stress than the metal around it.
Repeat that thousands of times and a microscopic crack appears. Engineers call it fatigue. It's like bending a paperclip back and forth: each bend is gentle, but eventually one breaks it.
Now round the corner. The flow of force glides around the curve and spreads out, with nowhere to crowd.
Same metal. Same pressure. Same number of flights. A completely different outcome.
Four years later, the Comet returned to commercial service, redesigned.
Modern airliner windows are rounded, and they have been ever since.
So the next time you look out of the window, remember: that gentle curve isn't decoration. It's a lesson learned at a terrible cost.
Sometimes the smallest shape on a machine is the story of everything that once went wrong.
